name: Weston A. Price diet
lead: The Weston A. Price diet is a traditional-foods way of eating drawn from dentist Weston A. Price (1870-1948), who compared the diets, teeth and facial development of traditional and Westernised populations in his 1939 book Nutrition and Physical Degeneration [2]. Followers say nutrient-dense whole foods support well-formed teeth and jaws, and that refined flour, sugar and industrial vegetable fats are linked to dental decay and poorer facial development, a theme that appeals to people interested in jaw and face structure.

The Weston A. Price Foundation, co-founded in 1999 by Sally Fallon and Mary G. Enig, promotes raw milk, animal fats such as lard, tallow and cod liver oil, lacto-fermented foods, bone broths and minimally processed or soaked grains [2][4]. Lifters on T Nation have cited Price when arguing for low-carbohydrate high-fat eating, animal foods and raw dairy [5][6].

Price's work was received with both praise and criticism, and critics have faulted the lack of quantitative dietary analysis and control groups [2]. No clinical trials of the diet as a whole were found.

paras: Price was born in Ontario in 1870, qualified in dentistry at the University of Michigan in 1893 and practised in Cleveland, Ohio. He chaired the National Dental Association between 1914 and 1928 and worked on dental radiography and porcelain furnace technology.[2]

He first studied dental disease through the lens of focal infection, arguing that infected and root-treated teeth could cause systemic illness. That theory later fell out of favour, and reviews in 1940 and 1951 criticised the methods behind it.[2] Around the 1920s he turned to nutrition, and Nutrition and Physical Degeneration (1939) compared groups including Swiss Alpine villagers, Native American, Polynesian, Pygmy and Aboriginal peoples, using many photographs.[2]

Price argued that Western diseases were rare among traditional peoples and rose as they adopted commercially processed foods, and he blamed refined flour, sugar and modern processed vegetable fats for deficiency, tooth decay and poor facial development.[2] Later organisations built dietary recommendations on these ideas; the Weston A. Price Foundation was co-founded in 1999 by Sally Fallon and Mary G. Enig.[2]

The Weston A. Price Foundation advocates access to certified raw milk, traditional fats such as lard, tallow, cod liver oil and olive oil, lacto-fermented dairy and vegetables such as sauerkraut, and bone stocks. It recommends unprocessed or minimally processed and organic foods and whole grains that are soaked or soured to reduce phytic acid and other anti-nutrients [4]. It takes a favourable view of saturated fat and opposes the lipid hypothesis [4].

A 1940 Canadian Medical Association Journal review called the book a masterpiece of research, and a 1950 Laryngoscope review compared Price to Charles Darwin. Other reviewers said some conclusions went beyond the evidence, and JAMA described him as observant but not wholly unbiased.[2]

A 1981 critique by William T. Jarvis argued that Price held a preconceived view of primitive health, lacked quantitative dietary analysis and overlooked malnutrition, high infant mortality and gum disease. Stephen Barrett, a consumer-health critic, likewise described Price's survey as superficial. The Weston A. Price Foundation has published a rebuttal.[2]

Quackwatch has called the foundation's dietary strategies questionable and Science-Based Medicine criticised its website, and Joel Fuhrman faulted it for not updating recommendations in light of contrary evidence [4]. An FDA official described its raw milk claims as false and unsupported, and the CDC and FDA state that pasteurization does not significantly change milk's nutritional value [4]. The foundation says it receives no government or agribusiness funding [4].
No studies found. The historical literature consists of Price's own observational surveys and later commentary, such as a 1950 Swiss journal article reviewing his work on diet and dental disease.[3]

lore.intro: Price's name comes up on T Nation in discussions of low-carbohydrate eating, animal foods and traditional diets.

claims.claim: Traditional diets built on animal fats produced healthier bodies than modern processed diets
claims.believers: One T Nation poster says the obese do well on low-carbohydrate high-fat eating and that Weston A. Price had this figured out decades ago [5]; another notes Price influenced the diet he follows [7].
claims.experts: Reviewers say Price's surveys lacked quantitative analysis and control groups, and the foundation's claims have been criticised by Quackwatch and Science-Based Medicine [2][4]. No trials of the diet as a whole were found.

claims.claim: Eating like traditional peoples supports jaw and dental development
claims.believers: Price's book compared photographs of traditional and Westernised groups and attributed facial changes to processed foods [2].
claims.experts: A 1981 critique by William T. Jarvis said Price held a preconceived view of primitive health and overlooked malnutrition and infant mortality [2].

card.summary: Traditional-foods philosophy from a 1930s dentist's travels; influential in diet circles, with no trials of the diet itself.
card.note: Based on Price's observational surveys, which later reviewers criticised for lacking controls.

quick.overview:
The Weston A. Price diet is a set of traditional-foods ideas drawn from dentist Weston A. Price's 1939 book comparing the teeth and faces of traditional and Westernised peoples. Followers connect refined sugar, flour and processed fats with dental decay and facial development.

Price's book drew early praise and later criticism for lacking quantitative analysis and controls. No clinical trials of the diet as a whole were found.
quick.mechanism: The central claim is that nutrient-dense traditional foods support normal tooth and jaw development, while processed foods cause deficiency. This is based on Price's observational comparisons, not on controlled experiments.
quick.risks: No specific harms were identified in the sources reviewed. Critics focus on the weak evidence base of Price's surveys and, separately, on his earlier focal infection theory, which was discredited by later reviews.

chain: Nutrient-dense traditional foods in place of refined foods
Proponents say better mineral and fat-soluble vitamin intake supports tooth and jaw development
Claimed result: well-formed teeth and broader facial structure
angle.text: Followers adopt the diet to support teeth, jaws and general health, following Price's photographic comparisons of traditional and Westernised peoples [2]. The facial-development link is Price's observation, not a trial finding.
